verification.note: The 1+1 mark split is a CLAIM, not the board's, until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. Unit 14 (Chemistry in Everyday Life) is sourced from the chemistry half of "FAST TRACK IPE for Sr. Students", book pp.105-106, printed chapter "11. CHEMISTRY IN EVERYDAY LIFE"; the book prints this question on book p.105 as VSAQ 6. Neither the two-book union check nor a board back-test was possible for Chemistry-II: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is physics-only and first-year, and no second-year chemistry paper is in the corpus. BOOK ERROR (book p.105, VSAQ 6): the printed answer reads "The drugs are produced by micro organism, which inhibit the growth (or) kill of micro-organisms are called antibiotics. Ex: Penicillin and chloramphenicol." The definition contradicts its own second example. Chloramphenicol was first obtained from a micro-organism but is now made by full chemical synthesis, so a definition restricted to substances produced by micro-organisms excludes the very drug the book names. The card uses the wider definition, produced wholly or partly by chemical synthesis, which is also the definition the syllabus uses, and adds the two conditions the book leaves out: the drug acts in low concentration, and it either kills the micro-organism or stops its growth. BOOK GAP: narrow spectrum and broad spectrum are not mentioned at all, although penicillin and chloramphenicol are the standard example of each. Both are named here.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The definition
lines: An antibiotic is a substance produced
wholly or partly by chemical synthesis
which, in low concentration, stops the
growth of a micro-organism or kills it.
steps.why: Two conditions carry this mark. The substance must act at low concentration, and it must either kill the micro-organism or stop its growth, because both count. Low concentration separates an antibiotic from a chemical that works only by being corrosive; what separates it from a disinfectant is that an antibiotic acts inside the body against the micro-organism, while a disinfectant is applied on a non-living surface. The older definition, produced by a micro-organism, is too narrow: chloramphenicol is made by full chemical synthesis.
common_mistakes: Writing that every antibiotic comes from a micro-organism. Chloramphenicol is made by chemical synthesis.
Leaving out the words low concentration. A substance that acts only in large amounts is not an antibiotic.
steps.memory_tip: Small dose, large effect: an antibiotic acts in low concentration.
steps.margin_note: Write low concentration in the definition. That phrase is what the examiner looks for.

steps.label: Examples and their spectrum

lines.text: Penicillin G is narrow spectrum: it acts

lines: on a few kinds of bacteria only.
acts on many kinds of bacteria.
steps.why: Spectrum means the range of bacteria a drug acts on. Penicillin G acts on a small range and is called narrow spectrum; chloramphenicol acts on a wide range and is called broad spectrum. Naming the spectrum beside each example is the extra line that turns a two-word answer into a full one.
common_mistakes: Writing that penicillin is broad spectrum. Penicillin G is narrow spectrum; ampicillin and amoxycillin are the broad spectrum members.
Giving dettol or formalin as antibiotics. Those are an antiseptic and a disinfectant.
steps.memory_tip: Narrow spectrum acts on few kinds; broad spectrum acts on many.
steps.margin_note: Two names finish this mark. Adding narrow and broad spectrum costs one line and completes the answer.

insider_note: Most students write only two drug names here. Add one line saying that penicillin is narrow spectrum and chloramphenicol is broad spectrum; that is the line that separates a full answer from a half one.
